Name: Lisa Pruett
Badge: Teacher as Researcher | Sustaining Literacy Routines
Looking back on this inquiry cycle, what did you learn about your teaching and your students that you might not have noticed otherwise? How did engaging in this teacher-research process shape or shift your thinking about your classroom practice?:

Looking back on this inquiry cycle, I learned that they struggle putting their thoughts into a structured piece of writing, as a science teacher, I don't notice these things as much because we don't spend a lot of time writing and I never compare articles. So this was hard for them and myself. Engaging in this teacher-research process helped shift my thinking about my classroom practice is that I know that I NEED to become stronger in this area for my students to be successful writers.

Think back to a moment during the lesson sequence that stands out. It could be a comment from a student, an unexpected challenge or success, a shift in engagement, or a moment when your own thinking changed. Describe what happened and why this moment feels meaningful to you now. What does it reveal:
A moment during this lesson sequence that stands out is when they watched the video and were able to form the connection of global warming on their own. This moment felt meaningful to me because its nice when you teach something, move on, and then they are able to recall and make a connection at a later time.
As you look over the drafts your students produced in this lesson sequence, what early patterns, surprises, or questions are emerging for you? As I look over the drafts my students produced in this lesson sequence, it surprises me to see how much students struggle with writing. I am most curious to explore how to be better at teaching writing for my students to be better at writing.
